articles.title: BNSF Demands Cloud Seattle's Path to Replacing Aging Jackson Street Bridges
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Aging segments of Seattle's downtown street grid around King Street Station would not be able to be rebuilt at their existing heights if they needed to be replaced, according to a newly released study from the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). A bridge over BNSF railroad tracks that carries South Jackson Street and Second Avenue Extension S would need to be three to seven feet higher to receive railroad buy in, a fact that would have cascading effects on access to other nearby streets and properties.

SDOT's study was part of its Bridge Replacement and Rehabilitation Program. It looked at the early 1900s-era S Jackson Street bridge between Third and Fourth Avenue – known as Bridge 7 – and another smaller bridge to the east in front of Union Station, known as Bridge 33W. Both bridges were rehabilitated in the 1980s, and seismically retrofitted to withstand earthquakes more recently.

Nonetheless, City engineers have determined both bridges have surpassed their design life and could ultimately need to be replaced. This is a significant challenge given the fact that they provide critical connections for people across Seattle and the entire region, with more than 1,400 buses traversing them every weekday.

"With regular maintenance and monitoring, many bridges last well beyond their design life but it is still important to plan ahead especially when the need for future rehabilitation and replacement is not driven by a poor bridge condition state," the study's executive summary states.

Any replacement bridge over the railroad tracks would need to be significantly higher than today's conditions because the existing bridge doesn't meet current requirements for vertical clearance above BNSF's right-of-way. Such a change would have major impacts on nearby properties, including an entrance to Sound Transit's Sounder commuter rail platform, and the King Street Station entrance plaza. Near bridge 33W, the Icon Apartments sit directly along the sidewalk, with a potential seven foot increase in height something that would block most of the ground floor.

"Improving the vertical clearance to meeting BNSF’s requirements would result in a grade rise of S Jackson Street between 3 and 7 feet, depending on the replacement concept," the summary states. "This change in grade would require 4th Avenue S to also be replaced and would affect access to properties adjacent to 4th Avenue S, S Jackson Street, and potentially along 2nd Avenue Extension S."

The cost of a replacement for Bridge 7 was pegged at anywhere from $99 million to $210 million, but any required height increase would also necessitate replacing Bridge 33W, at a cost of another $32 to $66 million. The study did look at what a retrofit for Bridge 7 would look like, but found that option would cost up to $160 million and take up to 12 years, due to a narrow window of construction work that BNSF would allow within its right-of-way – crews could only work four hours every day.

What it would look like to rebuild the Fourth Avenue S Viaduct was not addressed in the study, but those costs are likely to dwarf the costs of the smaller two bridges it sits between. In 2020, SDOT released the news that costs to seismically retrofit the Fourth Avenue bridge, from S Main Street south to Seattle Boulevard, had to be revised upward by a factor of more than 12, from $8.6 million to $109.4 million.

This cluster of interconnected bridges in south downtown has been in the crosshairs for a number of years, as Sound Transit has continued to advance alternatives for a second light rail tunnel through downtown as part of the Ballard Link Extension. It was partly the narrow construction window set by BNSF, on top of other potential technical hurdles, that have pushed Sound Transit away from considering a route under Fourth Avenue, with a third-party consultant calling the option "not reasonably constructible."

The need to retrofit these bridges has also been an issue in the context of the Center City Connector, with a 2024 study concluding that upgrades would be needed to handle the new, heavier streetcar vehicles that would be a component of bridging the city's existing streetcar lines together via First Avenue.
But even if Sound Transit passes the area by and the streetcar remains on ice, these bridges aren't getting any younger.

The $1.55 billion transportation levy that voters approved in 2024 included $221 million for bridges, but most of that funding was earmarked for bridge repair and maintenance, not any full bridge replacements. The levy set aside $20 million to be divvied up among six bridge projects in the hopes of seeking future construction funding, but higher priority bridges like the Magnolia Bridge, and the First and Fourth Avenue bridges further south in SoDo over the Argo railyard, made the cut ahead of Bridge 7 or 33W.

The City could save money on a replacement for Bridge 7 by building an arch bridge over the BNSF right-of-way, just four feet over the existing bridge – but that option was all but rejected due to its impact on traffic. The arch bridge concept would have been expected to cost between $68 million and $145 million, or $65 million less than the high-end cost for the full replacement.

"One concept included removal of the portion of the Bridge 7 structure under 2nd Avenue Extension S, south of S Jackson Street," the study summary noted. "However, preliminary traffic analysis showed that these changes to roadway network and circulation in the neighborhood would not be feasible with today’s bus and vehicle volumes."
The bridge planning study's executive summary stops short of making a recommendation, but SDOT's project website does go a step further in summarizing where things currently stand.

"While we have not selected a preferred alternative, bridge replacement is looking like it would be a better investment in the long-term," the newly updated webpage notes. "Any of the options will be expensive, require railroad coordination, take time to construct, and cause disruption to the surrounding neighborhoods. We will need to be creative and opportunistic in our approach to funding and delivering this project."

The state of these bridges is unlikely to become a live issue in the immediate future, but this study does put some major issues on the table that future generations of Seattle leaders are likely going to grapple with – and that could leave Jackson Street looking very different than it does today.

articles.title: Why Seattle waste drivers aren’t getting pricked like sanitation workers in New York (but you should still dispose of your needles in a safer way)
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Automated garbage can lifts mostly protect Seattle collection drivers as the city’s garbage and recycling systems deal with an increase in consumer hypodermic needle use.

Seattle Public Utilities tells CHS it has not recorded an increase in needlestick injuries among contractors servicing the city. Unlike cities where crews manually lift trash bags, Seattle’s residential routes use mechanical arms to empty curbside carts directly into trucks, keeping drivers away from thin bags and protruding needles.

Cities with manual collection face different hazards. In New York City, where Department of Sanitation crews lift bags by hand, the agency has logged 49 needlestick injuries through early August. That surpassed the 46 incidents reported in 2025 and rose from 18 in 2020. The increase led New York to raise fines for improper needle disposal from $100 to $250. DSNY does not test recovered needles, but officials attribute the rise to more residents using at-home injectable drugs.

Manual collection remains standard in older, denser East Coast cities where narrow streets and row homes prevent automated side-loader trucks from operating. In Philadelphia, the city’s Community Life Improvement Program and Department of Sanitation deploy specialized teams equipped with puncture-resistant gear to clear corridors like Kensington, where union representatives with AFSCME District Council 33 have cited worker safety and punctures from loose needles during manual trash collection. In Boston, where contracted haulers physically toss bags into rear compactors, city public health officials conduct targeted daily needle sweeps along high-traffic corridors like the “Mass and Cass” area to clear loose syringes before curbside collection begins.

The municipal strain follows a broader shift documented by The New York Times , which reported last month that syringes and auto-injectors have migrated from clinical settings directly onto domestic bathroom vanities. According to the report, nearly one in five U.S. adults has tried an injectable GLP-1 medication like Ozempic, while consumer interest in injectable peptides and at-home fertility treatments like IVF — which grew nearly 40% between 2018 and 2026 — has routinely pushed medical sharps into households.

That proliferation has created new hazards in our waste The New York Times reports sanitation workers there frequently encounter exposed, loose needles when lifting plastic garbage bags, with one New York City department supervisor telling the paper that crews regularly open bags to find needles completely unshielded. The surge is also hitting retail businesses. The Times cited a Nordstrom Rack restroom that posted signs pleading with shoppers to stop dropping GLP-1 syringes into its public sharps containers due to the escalating fees the retailer pays to empty them.

SPU says that it does not track the source or type of discarded needles, meaning it cannot link box totals to specific drugs like GLP-1 weight-loss medications. While automated trucks protect Seattle drivers, the machinery does not protect downstream workers.

Washington law and King County health rules prohibit sharps in household garbage or curbside recycling. SPU directs residents to use puncture-resistant containers and drop them at public boxes or the North Transfer Station.

Improperly discarded sharps still reach sorting plants. Industry publications note that because retail pharmacies rarely provide mail-back boxes with injectable prescriptions, people often throw pens into the trash or stash needles in milk jugs and soda bottles sent to recycling.

Compactors inside automated trucks crush those plastic jugs, scattering loose needles into the sorting stream. According to the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, needlestick wounds risk exposure to hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV.

The danger then falls on sorting facilities, where workers manually pull recyclables off conveyor belts. A study by the Environmental Research & Education Foundation and the Solid Waste Association of North America estimated somewhere around 1,000 needlestick injuries happen annually at recycling facilities, with manual sorters injured at a rate of 3.9 per 100 workers. More than half of surveyed facilities report finding loose needles mixed into recyclables daily or weekly.

A few drugmakers and select specialty pharmacies provide free mail-back sharps containers for specific injectables, but standard retail pharmacies rarely include disposal with prescriptions. As a result, safe disposal largely depends on state initiatives — such as Washington’s free prepaid injector mail-back service — and municipal drop-off sites provided by utilities like SPU.

Seattle’s tough years of drug crisis including spikes in intravenous drug use may be helping keep workers safe from the pricks. Seattle Public Utilities maintains 23 public drop boxes across the city for safe disposal. The disposal boxes, located on city property and public rights-of-way such as exterior restroom walls in parks like Cal Anderson , are heavy-duty, tamper-resistant deposit chutes. Residents drop sealed containers into the chute directly at any time.

Seattle’s drop boxes are also busier. SPU reports it collected 446,716 sharps through its 23 public drop boxes through the first half of 2026 — about 22% more than the pace in the previous two years. It’s unknown how many of the rest of those needles are taking a dangerous path to the landfill or recycling plant.
Learn more from King County Public Health on how to safely dispose of needles at home .

articles.title: At Sea’d In, the wood fire is burning again in Capitol Hill’s Chophouse Row
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: Two of the most important names in the Pike/Pine business community are behind the creation of Sea’d In , a new Capitol Hill restaurant that treats fish like fine steak.

Chef Heong Soon Park said the spark for the wood fire-powered concept came in a call from Chophouse Row developer Liz Dunn , who Park credits with keeping Capitol Hill’s character intact as the neighborhood changes and grows. She had a showcase restaurant space open and one question for him up front: Did he like cooking with fire?

Park had already been circling an idea for a seafood restaurant, something he had originally pictured closer to the water, but that concept never found the right home. When Dunn reached out, he brought the idea to her instead, and the two of them worked out the shape of it together. “She inspired me, and then I filled in the blanks,” he says.

While Dunn — Chophouse Row, the Piston & Ring Building, Melrose Market — is the shaper of many of the core commercial spaces of modern-day Capitol Hill, Park is responsible for a growing fleet of neighborhood restaurants.

Park’s first venture in Capitol Hill’s restaurant scene was Meet Korean BBQ which has been part of Capitol Hill since its inauspicious opening in the winter of 2020 only weeks before the COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns hit.

In 2024, Park took on the reinvention of a space that had been home to a deeply rooted Capitol Hill food legend with the transformation that saw his Grana Padano and Parmesan-laden Cheese Room take over the longtime Melrose at Pine home of Machiavelli as its ownership decided to focus on its Edmonds location.
Park’s most recent Capitol Hill reboot came last year on E Pike where he opened Gol Mok Korean Market Bar , a new start for the Taku space created by Seattle celebrity chef Shota Nakajima .
Other recent acquisitions include restarts in West Seattle including the Luna Park Cafe .
Park’s new beginnings aren’t shallow imitations. He has been part of the Seattle dining scene for 20 years and owns Chan in the Paramount Hotel downtown and the Bacco Café in Pike Place Market .

Sea’d In is also much more than a reboot. The restaurant’s identity is in dry-aged seafood and techniques Park traces back to South Korea where cooks didn’t have the cold storage geography of Europe and instead learned to age fish in the cold sea air.

Seafood comes in from auction and gets handled as little as possible before going into an aging room held between roughly 0 and 5 degrees Celsius, with humidity between 70 and 90%. Timing depends on the fish. White fish like snapper or branzino ages three to four days, salmon two to three weeks, and tuna, because of its higher fat content, as long as two months. It’s the same protein and enzyme breakdown that tenderizes dry aged beef, drawing out moisture and concentrating flavor.
From there, everything goes onto Sea’d In’s wood fired grill, the only cooking method in the space formerly home to the Light Sleeper wine bar and once home to long-gone Bar Ferdinand .

“We start with this basic fish, we layer it with the dry age, we layer it with the smoke, we layer with koji, we layer with the sauce,” Park says. That idea of stacking time and technique is where the restaurant’s “Time and Fire” comes from. Time is aging and fermenting. Then comes the fire.

Park says this project might be his favorite of anything he’s done, largely because of the Chophouse Row and its courtyard. There is live music on weekends, a monthly art night, and an annual local fashion show, plus neighbors like Xóm and Tailwind Cafe .
“This is exactly how Capitol Hill used to be. Nothing crazy, always chill, happy, relaxed,” he says. “Now I feel like I’m part of it.”
For a first visit, he recommends the crudo, all of it dry-aged, along with vegetables cooked over the wood fire and a whole fish that’s gone through the full aging and grilling process.
“Come in here or sit in the courtyard and enjoy the weather. You don’t have to be on your phone anymore,” Park says. “This is a good place to know neighbors. Meet actual people here.”
Sea’d In now open inside Chophouse Row at 1124 11th Ave. Learn more at seadinseattle.com .

articles.title: Seattle students head to class as district and teachers union reach agreement
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Seattle Public Schools and the Seattle Education Association reached a tentative contract agreement late Tuesday clearing the way for classes to begin on schedule Wednesday morning.

The deal averts a strike across the district which serves some 50,000 students and employs 6,000 union-represented educators and staff . Students in grades 1 through 12 return to classrooms on September 2, followed by preschool and kindergarten students on September 8 . The contract remains subject to ratification votes by both the union membership and the Seattle School Board .

Specifics of the tentative deal including final salary schedules were not disclosed in the joint announcement but the union said the sides reached “agreements” on all 52 issues raised in the negotiations.

The tentative agreement reportedly is centered on the district’s officer of an 8.8% baseline salary increase over three years, broken down into annual bumps of 2.6%, 3.6%, and 2.6%. This raise passes through projected state-funded cost-of-living adjustments with no furlough days, alongside standard annual experience step increases averaging roughly 4% for eligible staff.

CHS reported here on what was at stake as the district’s contract package would pass through projected state-funded cost-of-living adjustments with no local increase. The Seattle Education Association was proposing the same state inflation adjustment plus an additional 6.0% wage increase over three years, alongside targeted bumps for paraprofessionals and office staff.

Additional provisions including new psychologists, assigning a full-time social worker or counselor to schools with more than 350 students, and restructuring special education models to keep students in neighborhood schools with increased behavioral support were also on the table.
The district proposal also featured SPS-funded health accounts, reduced monthly staff meetings, and an additional paid training day for more than 1,500 paraprofessionals and office staff.

The negotiations follow the union’s previous three-year collective bargaining agreement reached in September 2022. That deal provided a 7% raise in year one, 4% in year two, and 3% in year three, alongside cost-of-living adjustments tied to the state Implicit Price Deflator. That established a 14% baseline wage increase over the life of the contract.
The median and average salary for Seattle Public Schools teachers sits at approximately $117,000 per year.

Seattle’s public school district is facing ongoing challenges amid falling enrollment. Enrollment is hovering around 49,000 students, representing a drop of roughly 4,500 to 5,000 students from its pre-pandemic peak of 53,627 in 2019–2020. Elementary buildings are currently operating at an average of roughly 65% capacity, well below the district’s 85% target. The primary driver of the long-term decline is smaller incoming classes.

The district’s plan to shutter under-enrolled elementary schools including Stevens Elementary on Capitol Hill was met with strong public backlash in 2024 but the economic factors driving the push have not improved.

The district is facing ongoing structural budget deficits, operating with an annual general fund budget of roughly $1.35 billion while managing annual shortfalls in the $90 million to $130 million range. The state allocates school funding primarily on a per-pupil model. With its enrollment dropping, SPS loses tens of millions annually in state basic education funding. Meanwhile, federal pandemic relief funds have fully expired.
Superintendent Ben Shuldiner praised the bargaining teams and SEA leadership for reaching an agreement that keeps classrooms safe and supportive while allowing schools to open on time.
“Educators are fierce advocates for our students and SEA members made this agreement possible through strength and unity,” SEA vice president and lead bargainer Davina Diaz said.

articles.title: The Ultimate ORCA Speedrun
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: At 9:59am last Friday, I boarded Everett Transit Route 29 at Everett Transit Mall Station. While the six other passengers on the bus were traveling to work, home, or somewhere else, for me this trip was the first segment of my region-wide ORCA speedrun. Transit speedrunning is the process of visiting every station in a transit system as fast as possible. In cities/regions with complex rail transit networks, such as San Francisco or New York , competitors look for new routes to beat the previous record. While the Link light rail system now has 3 lines across Puget Sound, the speedrun route is fairly straightforward . Our rail network is not complex enough to provide other potential routes that are faster. However, the broader ORCA network is quite complex.

One Regional Card for All (ORCA) powers transit fares for nine transit agencies across four counties in Washington. Visiting every stop in the ORCA network would take months, so the ORCA speedrun has a simpler goal: ride every mode of fixed-route transit offered by each agency in the ORCA pod, as fast as possible. This includes every type bus service, rail service, and ferry service from each of the nine agencies. For example, King County Metro offers three types of bus service: local, express, and RapidRide. Likewise, Kitsap Transit has both Fast Ferries and Foot Ferries. In total, there are 21 different modes across the nine agencies. Paratransit, dial-a-ride-transit, or other on-demand services are not included. City Beautiful and The Transit Bandit have completed similar speedruns using seven of the transit modes in Seattle.

Centered around downtown Seattle, ORCA is supported by agencies to the north, south, and west. For my speedrun, I started in the north (Everett) and planned to finish in the south (Tacoma). I shared updates in real-time on Bluesky and a full map of the run is available here .

Snohomish County has two dedicated transit agencies: Everett Transit (ET) and Community Transit (CT). ET is one of the smaller agencies on the list, it just runs local bus service. CT, meanwhile, has local bus routes, Express bus routes and Swift routes.

My trip on Route 29 checked the Everett Transit box. I got off the bus at the South Everett Freeway Station and transferred to an inbound Community Transit Express Route 905. Route 905 returned to I-5 and traveled directly to Lynnwood Transit Center. As I would need to return back to Lynnwood TC to board Link to get to Seattle, this next segment required an out-and-back using both Swift and a local route. I boarded the next Orange Line bus towards Edmonds College and took it one stop to Hwy 99. Thankfully, the traffic signal at Hwy 99 & 196th St was in my favor so I could catch the Lynnwood-bound Route 166 across the street with seconds to spare.

Link is the best option for traveling between Lynnwood and Seattle. The 40 minute ride was a nice opportunity to relax after a few very close transfers in Snohomish County. In Seattle, I had about an hour to ride five different modes: Metro bus, Metro Express bus, Seattle Streetcar, ST Express bus, and the Seattle Center Monorail. While I had planned most of the day, this hour was improvised. At Westlake station, I got off the 1 Line and walked over to the waiting South Lake Union streetcar. I hopped aboard and we departed a few minutes later. After two stops, I alighted the streetcar at Denny Way and boarded an eastbound Route 8 bus. As we sped down the new bus lane on Denny, I noticed a ST Express Route 577 bus was about to start its trip to Federal Way. I got off Route 8 after just one stop and ran to the bus stop at Boren Ave & Virginia St. The Route 577 bus arrived a few moments later, exactly on time.

I now had just two modes left for downtown Seattle: the Seattle Center Monorail and a Metro Express bus. Most Metro Express buses run during peak hours so my only option was Route 28X. I rode Route 577 a few stops to Stewart St & 7th Ave. After a short walk to Westlake Center Mall, I boarded a well timed monorail train and made my way to Seattle Center. I sat near the front of the train as I needed to make a quick exit to catch the next bus. A southbound Route 28X bus was scheduled to depart from 7th & Thomas at 11:52am, four minutes after the monorail arrived at Seattle Center. A four minute transfer is usually fine, but this bus stop was a 7 minute walk from the monorail station.

After a short jog I made it to the bus stop 2 minutes early (the bus was 1 minute late). I boarded the 28X bus to check off the last mode needed in downtown Seattle. My next scheduled ride was the 12:30pm West Seattle Water Taxi operated by King County Metro. With 25 minutes to spare I decided to ride Metro’s Waterfront Shuttle.

I arrived back at Pier 50 at 12:19 and joined the queue to board my first boat of the day. Metro’s West Seattle Water Taxi took just 10 minutes to reach Seacrest Dock. I boarded on DART Route 773 for a quick ride to Avalon Ave & Bradford, just south of the West Seattle Bridge. After crossing the street, I caught an inbound C Line bus back to downtown Seattle. This RapidRide bus was the fourth and final mode of the day from King County Metro.

The C Line bus sailed across the West Seattle Bridge and dropped me off across the street from the Seattle Ferry Terminal. After enjoying some of the ferry terminal amenities, we (my wife joined me for this section) boarded the Seattle – Bremerton Washington State Ferries route. The hour-long trip sailed by and we arrived in Bremerton at 2:39pm, just 9 minutes behind schedule. Despite the delay we had a few minutes for a delicious lunch at Mezcalitos. At 3:30p, we walked back over to the ferry terminal to catch the smallest boat of the day: a Kitsap Transit Foot Ferry to Annapolis. The Admiral Pete was packed to standing-room-only as we made the short trip to Annapolis. We alighted the vessel with everyone else and started to walk down the surprisingly long dock. When we were halfway to land, the boat’s engines roared to life and it sailed away. This was not the plan. We were supposed to take that same boat back to Bremerton. The 15-minute wait for the next sailing put the most important transfer of the day in jeopardy.

The next boat back to Bremerton was scheduled to get us back to Bremerton at 4:07pm. That would leave just four minutes to catch the 4:11pm Worker/Driver bus from the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard (PSNS). Worker/Driver buses run just once per day in each direction, so missing it would end this speed run attempt. After enjoying a private boat experience on the Foot Ferry trip back to Bremerton, I left the backpack with my wife and sprinted to PSNS. About a minute later, the retractable bollards descended and the Route 613 (Chico) bus rolled through the gate.

Kitsap Transit’s Worker/Driver routes are unique in Puget Sound. They travel from across Kitsap County to downtown Bremerton and PSNS. While they are designed for PSNS employees (and only PSNS employees can ride them within the facility), their one stop outside the PSNS gate makes them available to the public. I did confirm that these routes are open to the public with Kitsap Transit staff a few weeks ago. As the Worker/Driver routes travel long distances, they have far stop spacing. I rode Route 631 one stop (2.5 miles), to Kitsap Way & Marine Dr. Here, I had a lofty 10 minute transfer to Kitsap Route 212 back to the ferry terminal.

As luck would have it, Route 212 was running 17 minutes behind schedule and was scheduled to arrive at the Bremerton Terminal at 4:57pm. I needed to catch the 5:00pm Fast Ferry back to Seattle. As the Fast Ferry requires all passengers to be on board 2 minutes before departure, this would cut it way to close. Fortunately, there was a Route 226 bus from the same stop that was scheduled to arrive at the terminal at 4:55pm. Still too close for comfort, but I didn’t have another option. Route 226 arrived on time and I was finally heading back to the ferry terminal. While on board, I noticed the Route 226 had a slight detour in downtown Bremerton. Still worried about catching the Fast Ferry, I decided to get off the bus at Pacific and MLK Way and run the rest of the way. I met back up with my wife and we joined the line to board the Fast Ferry at 4:56pm.

The Fast Ferry was busy! Nearly every seat was occupied as we made the 30-minute trip back to Seattle. We got off the boat at 5:33pm, leaving just 12 minutes to catch the 5:45pm Sounder train to Tacoma. After saying goodbye to my wife, I ran through Pioneer Square to King Street Station.

At King Street Station, I boarded the 5:45pm S Line train bound for Lakewood. Unlike Link trains that afternoon , the Sounder train stayed on schedule and we pulled into Tacoma around 6:40pm. I crossed the street to board the T Line, the final Sound Transit service of the day. This left just two more transit modes: Pierce Transit local bus service and the Stream Community Line. Both local buses and the Stream Community Line serve the Pacific Ave corridor, so I exited the T Line train at Convention Center station and walked over to Pacific Ave & S 14th St. A Route 1 bus showed up first so I hopped aboard and rode it two stops to Pacific & 19th. After a few other buses came and went, the last southbound Stream Community Line bus for the day stopped at Pacific & 19th.

I boarded the final bus of the speedrun and took it one stop to Tacoma Dome station. After alighting the bus I stopped the timer to record the first ever ORCA speedrun time: 9 hours, 12 minutes, and 40 seconds.

I really enjoyed spending the day exploring cities across Puget Sound and observing how different transit services are used. The passengers and drivers I spoke with were extremely kind and helpful. I was most surprised by the Kitsap Transit ferries. Every ferry trip I observed was on-time and busy (except for the return trip from Annapolis). Given the geography, the ferries offer a shortcut across the water. These smaller (and cheaper) vessels can provide better service than WSF at a fraction of the cost. More cities and counties should be allowed to operate a fleet of passenger-only ferries. The 35% service reduction in the Seattle – Bremerton Fast Ferry route is incredibly disappointing.

Another highlight of the trip was seeing how an agency’s various transit services benefit the various types of trips. No transit mode is one-size-fits-all so agencies need to adapt the vehicle types (train, bus, boat) to fit their needs. One example of this was in Lynnwood, where Route 166 and the Orange Line cover the same route between Hwy 99 and Lynnwood Transit Center. Despite sharing the same road, the Orange Line only has one stop while Route 166 has four. The Route 166 bus I was on let passengers on/off at three of the four stops. These passengers would have been overlooked with only Orange Line service and Orange Line trips would be much slower with many more stops. The overlapping local and Swift service complement each other nicely. Pierce Transit uses a similar strategy on Pacific Ave with Route 1 and the Stream Community Line.
Here is the complete list of transit services included in the ORCA speedrun:

While most transit agencies in the ORCA pod offer more flexible transit options, the ORCA speedrun only includes fixed route transit. This is primarily to minimize the impact on other transit riders. Flexible services, such as Metro Flex, CT’s Zip Shuttle, or PT’s Runner service, have limited resources. Someone using those services for a speedrun could cause a longer wait for someone else. Fixed route options are acceptable because the impact of one extra rider is negligible.

While planning this adventure I went back and forth on including King County Metro shuttle routes. Metro operates four shuttle routes, but only one (Valley Shuttle) operates year-round. The other three (Waterfront, Golden Gardens, and the snow shuttle) are seasonal or weather dependent. To add another wrinkle, this is an ORCA speedrun and the Waterfront Shuttle is completely free. Ultimately, I decided to make shuttle routes optional.

Also, I chose to separate the T Line from the 1 Line and 2 Line. While they are all technically part of Link, the T Line has little in common with the 1 Line and 2 Line. Another reason to separate the Link lines: Sound Transit reports T Line ridership data to the FTA separate from the 1 Line and 2 Line.
If you plan on attempting this challenge, I hope you can beat my time. Here are a few other rules I followed:

I hope my successful speedrun inspires other Seattle transit enthusiasts to try it as well. While Link receives more of our collective attention than any other mode, trains, buses, and boats throughout Puget Sound play a critical role in getting people where they need to go. Riding each mode is a great way to understand the value it provides to its passengers and to the overall network.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Seattle Press Are Concocting a False Narrative to Undermine Mayor Wilson
articles.author: Maggie Block
paras: I am losing my mind consuming the local news coverage of the Seattle Center shooting and its aftermath.

I want to be clear right at the top, that I believe the job of the media, of journalism, is to hold those in power accountable. And if local broadcast and legacy media want to focus on holding our progressive city leaders to account, on legitimate concerns – crucially, in a way balanced with how they cover business-focused “moderate” politicians – I will welcome them with open arms.
But KIRO and KOMO’s coverage of Mayor Katie Wilson’s office in general, and after the Bite of Seattle shooting in particular, is something they need to be held accountable for.

On Monday, KIRO's newly installed news director, Jennifer Dahl, sat on a panel at Scenius Social billed as a conversation about art and Seattle's creative community. Twice, she turned the conversation toward Mayor Wilson and the communication failure after the Seattle Center shooting, a failure the mayor has already admitted.
Dahl warned that it could "happen again," invoking a mass shooting in Oregon.
Nothing sharpens a narrative quite like fear.
And I’m loath to admit it, but the failure was real.
However, Wilson has apologized. She asked the city's independent Inspector General to reconstruct what happened, figure out why it happened, and recommend how to prevent it from happening again.

I know that is something we rarely see from political leaders, so I can understand why a lay person may not know how to identify it. But professional journalists should know: that’s what accountability looks like.
Accountability is not turning one mistake into an albatross and hanging it around a woman's neck until Election Day.
Three people died at Seattle Center. A two-year-old was wounded. Families are grieving. Workers who tried to save lives are carrying images I imagine they would give anything to forget.
And somehow the great political question emerging from all of this has become: Why wasn't the mayor standing behind a microphone sooner?

Had the press conference happened exactly on time, three people would still be dead. The failure was in communicating about the response, not the response itself. Those are different things. Turning them into the same thing is not journalism happening naturally. It is an editorial choice. Then Dahl suggested the city should "turn on the Flock cameras."

Except, Seattle doesn't have Flock cameras . It has CCTV operated by the vendor Axon . Further, I am confused as to what Dahl imagines surveillance cameras could have done, as there were police officers standing roughly four paces from the shooters at Bite of Seattle.
How could a camera have stopped what armed police officers standing feet away could not?
This is how consent gets manufactured. Not through some smoky-room conspiracy where editors decide what you're allowed to believe. It's much more ordinary than that.

They decide what matters. Three people are killed, and yet the delayed press conference becomes the story. A delay of a few hours, confusion, questions about who was in charge, repeated again and again, until a single detail hardens into a verdict: City Hall is dysfunctional.

After that, the story begins feeding itself. A disagreement between SPD and the mayor becomes more evidence. A few councilmembers sharply criticize her and now there are "growing questions about her leadership." Then somebody commissions a poll asking voters whether they're worried about her leadership, and suddenly the media is reporting a public perception it helped manufacture.
Every individual fact can be true while the story constructed from them is bullshit.
Because a mayor arriving late to a podium is television.

The slow, boring, desperately important work of preventing the next shooting, youth programs, housing, coordination, intervention, mental health care, and the unglamorous labor of keeping people alive, isn't.
Our housing crisis did not begin in January. Homelessness did not begin in January. Public safety problems did not begin in January. Neither did government communication failures.

I remember 2020, after Lorenzo Anderson was shot during CHOP, when Seattle Fire waited nearby while police and fire struggled to coordinate their response. Mayor Jenny Durkan privately called what happened "foreseeable and avoidable" and ordered her chiefs to make sure it didn't happen again.
I don't mention that to excuse Wilson's mistake. Trust me, I have plenty of criticisms of my own for Seattle’s mayor. I mention it because history did not begin the morning Katie Wilson became mayor.
If communication breakdowns after deadly violence happened under previous administrations, then somebody should explain why this failure proves something uniquely rotten about this one.
Otherwise we're not applying a standard, but constructing one.
If one listens to local news lately and you'd think somebody handed Katie Wilson the keys to a perfectly functioning Seattle and she totaled it pulling out of the parking lot.

Take Starbucks. Recent coverage has asked whether layoffs at the company prove Seattle has become hostile to business. Except Starbucks cut roughly 2,000 corporate jobs across two rounds in 2025, before Wilson was mayor, as part of a turnaround strategy that began the previous September and sought billions in cost reductions.
That is a multinational corporation following its own restructuring plan.
It is not eight months of Katie Wilson's mayoralty somehow reaching backward through time.
Since we're suddenly so worried about Seattle's "business climate," when exactly do we get a nightly segment about the climate for workers?

You know, the people wondering whether they can pay rent. Buy groceries. Afford childcare. Keep living in the city where they work. Why does their anxiety always seem to be less newsworthy than a shareholder's?

The same thing happened with the recall petition filed by a married couple who also happened to have voted for her opponent last November. Every responsible outlet acknowledged it has little chance of surviving judicial review. In fact, the couple rescinded their recall filing this week, as the effort ran into the buzzsaw of a skeptical judge at its first hearing. But politically, it doesn't have to survive. It just has to consume oxygen.

That's how a housing affordability press conference becomes a press conference about the recall, while universal school meals , junk-fee protections and restrictions on surveillance-based dynamic grocery pricing struggle for the same attention.

Councilmember Bob Kettle held his own public safety press conference just before the mayor signed a set of executive orders accelerating Vision Zero . Seattle had 27 traffic deaths in 2025, including 18 pedestrians, compared with 37 homicides. Different causes. Similar human stakes.
Yet one produces weeks of breathless coverage while the other mostly produces passing mention and sad little roadside memorials we drive past on the way to work. Why?

That makes her human. It does not automatically make her uniquely incompetent. There has never been a flawless executive leader, anywhere. Certainly not in Seattle. And I have never seen the broadcast news concoct such a grandiose story around mayoral incompetence, despite far more deserving examples.
So it’s time to start asking questions of the people asking the questions.
Why does the business owner get the microphone while the worker disappears?
Why is the person demanding more cameras treated as an authority on safety while the person who will be watched by those cameras gets called an activist?

articles.title: Link Ends Earlier, Starts Later
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: Several comments have raised concerns that the August 29th service change shortened Link’s service day, so that it now ends earlier and starts later. This interacts with the launch of ST Express “Night Ride” routes between midnight and 4am. These theoretically can replace Link trips. But the ST Express routes bypass several high-ridership Seattle Link stations. This can force trips that were on Link in the midnight hour or 11 pm hour or 4 am hour to an ST Express or Metro route, turn a 1-seat ride into a 2-seat ride, and the bus routes are less frequent than Link was.

I wanted to know, did the spans really change on August 29? What is the current situation on weekdays, Saturdays, and Sundays? What kinds of trips at what hours are newly 2-seat rides? Where is the best place to live to have the earliest or latest Link service? Which can you go to on those lucky runs?

I looked at the new 1 Line and 2 Line schedules to quantify the current situation and changes. To reach these pages from Sound Transit’s website, use the schedule form on the home page to get to the interactive charts. To get a PDF of the schedule, go to the bottom of the page and press the “Full Schedule PDF” button.
I tried to make a consolidated list that would organize the first/last runs in different areas and days. But it was an insanely difficult job, and after a few hours I gave up.
So instead we’re going to crowdsource the issue.

How has Link’s span changed since August 29th? Has this affected your trips? Or do you see other people’s trips that are affected? Can you glean more from the schedules than I can? Can you figure out the right questions to ask AI to figure it out? (If you do, please disclose AI’s role in the result.)

Some of these impacts have already come up in recent articles’ comments, but this article is a place to consolidate them all together so we can see the total impact. And it will be a reference in the future when people have a question, so that they can find it all in one easy-to-find place.

The problem I had with the interactive schedule pages was I had to keep scrolling four directions to get at the first or last full run and short run, and when that would get you to Westlake or SeaTac or the final terminus. I had to keep going up to the date switcher. I kept finding mistake after mistake in my results, so I had to go back and reconfirm them, or compare weekday to Saturday again, and make sure I hadn’t jumped back to a date before the service change. Reading the PDFs online was a lot of up-and-down scrolling with similar printing. Printing the PDFs to get a wider-area view at once would take 34 pages per line. Maybe ST has a printed schedule book with them but I’d have to go search for a copy. I didn’t want to publish a list with mistakes that would waste everybody’s time.
Maybe if different people address small parts of the issue individually, we can get those facts more accurately and a better idea of the whole.

ST in the future wants to shorten Link’s span further, or have more single-track reductions, or more weekend closures of segments, to increase the time available for maintenance. We desperately want ST to increase maintenance because Link’s reliability is far below peer cities’ networks. This causes passengers to get stuck en route, be late for appointments, or drive to critical appointments to avoid the risk that Link will hiccup that day. It also snares visitors and gives them a negative impression of Seattle and Seattle’s transit. So we really want maintenance to be increased to make Link more reliable.

At the same time we need Link’s late-night and early-morning service. If ST Express night owls bypass several Seattle stations in the shoulder hours Link used to provide, then it’s not an adequate substitute. ST says Metro has night owl buses in all those areas (7, 36, 49, 67, 70). But those night runs are funded by Seattle’s transit levy, and will go away if voters don’t renew the levy this November. Metro stopped funding Seattle night owls in the 2014 recession. Also, the bus routes are half-hourly or hourly, as opposed to Link’s 15 minutes. If you switch to say the 49+597 or 36+597 to workaround the loss of Link, you may be waiting 30+30 minutes or a full hour.

This affects people coming home from bars, staff working at bars, people who start or end a night shift, people going to the airport for an early-morning flight, and people coming from an evening flight that was delayed and didn’t land until midnight or later, and airport workers with early-morning shifts.

So what are the actual problems now? Did Link’s span decrease August 29th? What kinds of trips, where, and when are affected? If in the future ST ends Link even earlier at 10pm or 9 pm every day or on monthly maintenance days or two-week maintenance periods, how big a deal would that be? How would we cope with it? What should we tell Sound Transit and our politicians about all this?

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.title: Beacon Hill Garden Drops Cesar Chavez's Name as South Park Weighs Park Renaming
paras: Update : After this article was published, Seattle Parks and Recreation announced on Sept. 2 that the City-managed park formerly known as Cesar Chavez Park will be named Parque Libertad. The article has been updated to reflect this new information.

For years, several South End locations bore the name of prominent Latino labor leader Cesar Chavez. But months after news reports detailed allegations that Chavez had sexually abused young women and teenagers, local sites have either been renamed or are being considered for new names.

Community leaders were initially shocked and unsure how to address the various places that honored him, including a garden at El Centro de la Raza in Beacon Hill and a city-managed park in South Park. Chavez's name and image were also found in a museum dedicated to Latino history in Washigton state.

In March, an investigation by The New York Times found that Chavez, a labor and Latino civil rights activist who advocated for farm workers and led national boycotts, had groomed and sexually assaulted numerous girls from 1972 to 1977. The investigation also found that he had sexually assaulted Dolores Huerta, a fellow labor leader who cofounded the United Farm Workers with Chavez. Chavez died in 2013.

At El Centro, the garden had a banner that bore Chavez's name. Veronica Gallardo, the director of facilities and cultural events at El Centro, said that after news of the allegations broke, his name was covered with tape, upon which someone wrote, "We stand with Dolores."
When the banner was altered, Gallardo said El Centro knew something needed to be done, so the organization removed the name and started thinking about what to call the garden.
"You have to really be thoughtful in the process," Gallardo said.
At first, Gallardo said El Centro considered naming the garden after Huerta but ultimately settled on "El Centro Demonstration Garden" because it better represented the local community.
"The demonstration garden is a community garden, so it was really important for us to just rename it 'El Centro Demonstration Garden,' because that's what it is."

The garden at El Centro is maintained by volunteers through the King County Master Gardener Program, a branch of the Washington State University Extension Program. Food harvested from the garden is used for the food bank. The garden also hosts a variety of educational opportunities and community events.
El Centro said in a March statement that it would remove public art throughout Roberto Maestas Plaza along with images of Chavez displayed on traditional altars.

After the investigation was published, places across the United States began removing Chavez's name or considering new names. The state of California renamed Cesar Chavez Day to Farm Workers Day, and Austin , Texas, is considering renaming a street.

The Sea Mar Museum of Chicano/a Latino/a Culture in South Park is dedicated to telling the stories of Latinos/as in Washington state. Erasmo Gamboa, the museum's curator, said that when the allegations against Chavez surfaced, the museum immediately worked to remove almost everything with his name or image.

"It was devastating when the country learned about this, because we have very few icons," Gamboa said. "No person, man or woman, should be excused for what Chavez did to these young people and to Dolores Huerta. I mean, that is just outright inexcusable."

But while the museum's focus was never on Chavez, Gamboa said his efforts inspired numerous farmworker movements in Washington, many of which were grassroots campaigns led by University of Washington students and community members.

Chavez spent little time in Washington, Gamboa added. He spoke at a rally at Garfield High School on Dec. 19, 1969. Earlier that day, Chavez had led a picket outside a Safeway in the University District and was named a First Citizen of Seattle by Mayor Wes Uhlman.
"To me, the more important thing is not Chavez himself, but … what farm-working people experienced in Washington state, and we're going to continue to focus on that," Gamboa said.
In South Park, a small park at 700 S. Cloverdale St., under Highway 99, was named after Chavez. The land is owned by King County but managed by Seattle Parks and Recreation.

Shortly after the investigation was published, the city took down signs with Chavez's name. Seattle City Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck and King County Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda have pushed for the park to be named after Huerta.
On Sept. 2, the park's new name was announced : Parque Libertad.

"Libertad (“freedom”) is a universal value that reflects the enduring pursuit of civil rights, equality, and opportunity for all," said Michele Finnegan, Seattle Parks and Recreation interim superintendent. "Parque Libertad honors the many individuals and communities who have advanced justice throughout Seattle’s history while creating a welcoming, inclusive place that celebrates freedom, belonging, and civic participation for future generations”

The city's park naming policy states that name changes can occur only if the individual's character does not serve the best interest of the community or conflicts with the department's mission and values.

The name change for the park occured after an administrative process involving both the city and county rather than through legislation. Any proposed names had to meet certain criteria, such as having historical or cultural significance or reflecting the geography of the area. Names could also honor indidivuals who have been deceased for at least three years or who made significant contributions to parks, recreation, or culture in the local community.

Community members were invited to provide input to the parks naming committee by April 14. Approximately 120 submissions were submitted, according to the city parks department. The committee reviewed suggestions and submited a recommendation to the superintendent of Seattle Parks and Recreation, who will made the final naming decision.
The city parks department made the announcement about the park's new name on Sept. 2.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?

articles.title: The Best Seafood Restaurants in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Seattle is synonymous with seafood, and anyone who visits from out of town naturally wants to know where the city’s best seafood is. But that’s a tricky question. There are some self-described “seafood restaurants,” but fish and shellfish work their way into nearly every menu around Puget Sound. This includes oysters on the half shell at too many happy hours to count, crab and geoduck served as high-end delicacies, and sandwiches where freshly caught salmon or tuna is the star ingredient. A “best seafood in Seattle” map would pretty much just be a map of Seattle. So consider this a sampler platter of some of what the city has to offer across several different styles of cuisine and price point.
